source: Sutton & Barto (2018/2020) Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, ch. 8 (Dyna, Dyna-Q+, prioritized sweeping)
finding: Dyna-Q runs one learning loop on both real and simulated experience. Planning steps (n per real step) run in the background, so the agent stays reactive and also deliberative. Founding theory: Sutton 1990/1991.
numbers: Example 8.1 Dyna maze: 47 states, gamma 0.95, alpha 0.1, epsilon 0.1, 30 repetitions. n=0 (plain one-step Q-learning) needed about 25 episodes to reach near-optimal. n=5 needed about 5 episodes. n=50 needed about 3 episodes. First episode about 1700 steps for all n.
quote: In Dyna-Q, learning and planning are accomplished by exactly the same algorithm, operating on real experience for learning and on simulated experience for planning.
limits: Tabular, deterministic, tiny maze. Parameters tuned for the n=0 agent. Sutton's original 1991 paper was not retrievable (host returned an error page), so it is known here only via the book and citing papers.
agent_relevance: Offline replay buys most of its value in the first few episodes after a new fact. A scaffold that replays stored traces between tasks should expect big early gains, then diminishing returns.

source: Sutton & Barto (2018/2020) Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, ch. 8 (Dyna, Dyna-Q+, prioritized sweeping) - Blocking and Shortcut mazes
finding: A Dyna-Q model goes stale when the world changes. In the Blocking Maze it eventually finds the new path. In the Shortcut Maze plain Dyna-Q never finds the new shorter path, because its own model says there is none and more planning makes it less likely to explore. Dyna-Q+ adds a bonus (reward r plus kappa times the square root of tau) in planning for transitions untried for tau steps, and does find the shortcut.
numbers: Blocking Maze: environment changes at step 1000. Shortcut Maze: changes at step 3000. Dyna-Q+ also allows never-tried actions to be planned over and models them as leading back to the same state.
quote: The more it planned, the less likely it was to step to the right and discover it.
limits: Average curves from the book, not tested statistically. The bonus is a heuristic with a small tuned kappa. The book says there is probably no solution that is both perfect and practical.
agent_relevance: Replay over a stored model can lock in old beliefs. For our subgoal library: add an age or staleness bonus so old entries get re-tested, otherwise replay only reinforces what is already believed.

source: Moore & Atkeson (1993) Prioritized sweeping: reinforcement learning with less data and less time. Machine Learning 13:103-130
finding: Prioritized sweeping keeps a priority queue of states. A state with a big value change pushes its predecessors onto the queue by priority, so a fixed number of backups per observation goes where it matters. It needs fewer observations and less real time than Q-learning and Dyna variants.
numbers: Table 2 (observations until 98% of decisions optimal), stochastic mazes: 2627 states Dyna-PI+ 240,000, optimistic Dyna 155,000, prioritized sweeping 94,000; 4528 states 525,000 / 310,000 / 200,000. Table 4, 14,400-state rod-in-maze, 100 backups per observation: Q never converged, Dyna-PI+ never, optimistic Dyna 55,000, prioritized sweeping 14,000 experiences. With 300 backups per observation on the 4528-state maze: optimistic Dyna 143,000 observations (3 hours) vs prioritized sweeping 21,000. Prioritized sweeping used about half the real time of Dyna.
limits: Each table cell is one run (the authors report little variance on repeats). Discrete states, 1990s hardware. The Dyna comparisons needed an optimism heuristic to explore at all. Peng & Williams (1993) Queue-Dyna was a simultaneous independent invention.
agent_relevance: Replay order matters more than replay amount. Rank which stored subgoals to re-run by how much the last outcome surprised us, and push the change to their predecessors.

source: Russek, Momennejad, Botvinick, Gershman, Daw (2017) Predictive representations can link model-based RL to model-free mechanisms
finding: SR-TD (successor representation learned by TD) solves reward revaluation and latent learning with no extra computation but cannot solve transition revaluation (detour) or policy revaluation. SR-MB (recompute M from a learned one-step model) solves transition revaluation but is on-policy and fails the new policy revaluation task. SR-Dyna replays stored (s,a,s') samples offline, updating the SR off-policy with the best next action, and solves all three if enough replay is done.
numbers: Grid-world simulations, median over runs. SR-Dyna: 10 one-step samples drawn with recency-weighted probability after each step. After a change, k samples were replayed: k=10 (insufficient) or k=10000 (sufficient). Same k used for Dyna-Q.
quote: Without sufficient replay, its performance degrades to that of SR-TD
limits: Pure simulation. This paper does NOT fit human data; it only gives behavioural predictions. Tabular, uniform random replay with recency bias, no realistic replay dynamics.
agent_relevance: Three kinds of change need three kinds of repair. A change of values (reward) is cheap. A change of structure (transition) or of which choices we would make (policy) needs real replay work. The scaffold should label which kind of change a failed check signals before choosing how much to re-run.

source: Russek, Momennejad, Botvinick, Gershman, Daw (2017) Predictive representations can link model-based RL to model-free mechanisms - Dyna-Q vs SR-Dyna under limited replay
finding: Key dissociation. With too little replay Dyna-Q degrades to a model-free agent and fails ALL revaluation tasks. SR-Dyna with too little replay degrades only to SR-TD: it still passes reward revaluation and latent learning but fails transition and policy revaluation. So a partial-replay agent keeps some flexibility if its cached object is a predictive map, not a one-step value.
numbers: Fig 6: both algorithms pass all 3 tasks with sufficient samples. With k=10: Dyna-Q passes none of the 3, SR-Dyna passes latent learning (and reward revaluation).
quote: Dyna-Q degrades to a model-free agent and it cannot pass any revaluation task
limits: Prediction only. The paper proposes testing it by manipulating rest length or distractor tasks, but reports no such human test.
agent_relevance: Cache what stays useful under a change, not just the final answer. A stored 'what follows what' map keeps working after a reward-type change even if no time was left to replay.

source: Russek, Momennejad, Botvinick, Gershman, Daw (2017) Predictive representations can link model-based RL to model-free mechanisms - discussion of replay-disruption evidence
finding: The paper argues rodent replay-blocking results are consistent with both Dyna-Q and SR-Dyna, which predict slower policy change. It notes human work without replay manipulation shows people are worse at transition and policy revaluation than reward revaluation, fitting SR-TD or SR-Dyna with limited backups. It also says exclusive reliance on replay for all flexibility seems unrealistic.
numbers: Qualitative discussion; cites Momennejad human data for the asymmetry.
limits: The human claim is indirect. At the time, replay manipulation had not been combined with the three revaluation tasks.
agent_relevance: Do not assume all flexibility comes from replay. Keep a cheap on-line component and a replay component, and test which carries a given gain.

source: Momennejad, Russek, Cheong, Botvinick, Daw, Gershman (2017) The successor representation in human reinforcement learning. Nature Human Behaviour 1:680-692 - Experiment 1
finding: Passive learning task, three within-subject conditions. Humans revalue after a reward change more than after a transition change, and both more than control. A pure model-based learner predicts no gap and a pure SR predicts no switch after transition change. Human behaviour was best captured by a hybrid SR-MB account.
numbers: n=58. Revaluation score: reward 0.5199 (SEM .0203), transition 0.4503 (SEM .0229), control 0.0310 (SEM .0310). Reward > transition t(57)=2.89 p<.01. Reward > control t(57)=10.14 p<.001. Transition > control t(57)=9.05 p<.001. Control not different from 0, t(57)=1.2 p=.22. Response time slower in transition than reward condition t(57)=2.08 p<.05.
limits: The gap between reward and transition revaluation (about 0.07) is small next to the main effects. The hybrid is described as a rough proxy for multi-system interactions. Online sample.
agent_relevance: Humans, like Dyna, are not fully flexible. Do not expect a cache-and-replay agent to repair structural changes as well as value changes without extra effort.

source: Momennejad et al. (2017) The successor representation in human reinforcement learning - Experiment 2 (sequential decision, with policy revaluation)
finding: Experiment 2 replicates experiment 1 in an active decision task and adds policy revaluation. Switching was highest for reward revaluation, lower and similar for transition and policy revaluation, and near zero in control.
numbers: n=88. Proportion who changed preference: reward .6591 (SEM .0505), transition .4659 (SEM .0532), policy .5000 (SEM .0533), control .0795 (SEM .0288). Reward vs transition Wald Z=-2.85 p=.0034. Reward vs policy Z=-2.61 p=.0043. Transition vs policy Z=.56 p=.577. Each vs control p<.0001.
limits: Single probe trial per participant. Conditions between subjects.
agent_relevance: Same as above. Policy-type repairs are as hard for humans as structural repairs.

source: Momennejad et al. (2017) - what the 'SR-Dyna fit best' label actually rests on
finding: Correction to the one-line summary that SR-Dyna fit human revaluation best. In the human-data paper the fitted models are pure MB, pure SR and a hybrid SR-MB (parameters b, w, sigma-squared, leave-one-out cross-validated log likelihood). SR-Dyna is described only as one speculative way to build the hybrid. No formal fit of SR-Dyna is reported there.
numbers: Hybrid model has 3 free parameters (b, w, sigma2); SR and MB have 2 each. Experiments n=58 and n=88.
quote: These different realizations of an SR-MB hybrid are essentially speculative in the absence of direct evidence.
limits: Evidence-status flag for this subfield: the best fit is a hybrid mixture of SR and model-based, not SR-Dyna itself.
agent_relevance: Treat SR-Dyna as a hypothesis class (cache plus mix with on-demand simulation), not a proven human algorithm. Do not mark it [E] in the schema.

source: Momennejad (2020) Learning structures: predictive representations, replay, and generalization. Curr Opin Behav Sci 32:155-166
finding: The review says human retrospective revaluation was best captured by a model that learned successor representations by both direct and replayed experience (SR-Dyna), and that SR-Dyna outperforms MF, MB, MF-MB, Dyna-Q(+), prioritized Dyna and SR without replay. Table 1 lists four replay algorithms: Dyna-Q (fast, misses new shortcuts), Dyna-Q+ (finds shortcuts, needs many samples), prioritized sweeping (PE-tagged predecessors), SR-Dyna (human-like retrospective revaluation, discrete states).
numbers: Review, no new data. Cites Russek 2017 and Momennejad 2017 for the claim.
limits: The primary human data paper fits MB, SR and hybrid, not the full list named here (see a08). The claim is stronger than the primary papers show.
agent_relevance: The SUBFIELDS table line comes from this review. It is a fair summary of the field's consensus but a weak evidence base; cite primary data instead.

source: Momennejad, Otto, Daw, Norman (2018) Offline replay supports planning in human reinforcement learning. eLife 7:e32548
finding: fMRI study of a 2-stage reward revaluation task. People change the stage-1 choice after stage-2 rewards change (revaluation) but not in a matched control. Cortical evidence for the stage-1 stimulus category during 30 s rest periods predicts how much people replan, only in revaluation blocks.
numbers: n=24. Replanning magnitude: revaluation t(23)=4.89 p<.0001; control t(23)=-0.10 p=.92; difference t(23)=4.333 p=.0002. Replay-replanning correlation: revaluation Spearman rho=0.54 p=.0068; control rho=-0.13 p=.55; difference by bootstrap p=.0230. Design: 4 blocks (2 revaluation, 2 control), each noiseless or noisy rewards, three 30 s rests inside relearning.
quote: offline replay of trajectories facilitates integrating representations that guide decisions
limits: Small n. Replay inferred from MVPA classifier evidence for a stimulus category (faces vs scenes) at rest, not from sequence decoding. Correlational, no replay manipulation. No main effect of reward noise.
agent_relevance: Evidence that replay between episodes helps integrate separate facts into a changed plan. Supports a consolidation step between task stages, only when there is something to integrate.

source: Momennejad et al. (2018) eLife - prioritisation by prediction error
finding: Second hypothesis: unsigned prediction errors tag memories for later replay, borrowed from prioritized sweeping. Noisy-reward control blocks (constant surprise, no actionable news) showed that surprise alone did not change preference. The paper stresses that replay is not by itself sufficient for a change: it helps only if the replayed experience supports one.
numbers: Abstract states neural sensitivity to uncertainty predicts subsequent replay and replanning; individual statistics for this link were not extracted.
limits: Model-based fMRI, n=24, correlational.
agent_relevance: Surprise is a trigger for re-running, but a re-run helps only if it can change the answer. This matches guardrails G1 (doubt only on a signal) and G2.

source: Mattar & Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay. Nature Neuroscience 21:1609-1617
finding: Normative extension of Dyna. Each replay backup has an Expected Value of Backup, EVB = Gain x Need. Gain is the policy improvement at the updated state. Need is expected future visits to that state. Greedy ordering by EVB gives reverse replay after a surprise (gain dominates) and forward replay before a run (need dominates). It learns faster than uniform-replay Dyna and a model-free agent in a Sutton Dyna-maze and a linear track.
numbers: Fig 1d: prioritised replay needs fewer steps per episode than random-replay Dyna and model-free in both environments. Backups with zero gain or zero need have zero utility. Model reproduces published rodent replay patterns (Ambrose 2016, Wu 2017 data).
quote: a backup that has no effect on behavior has zero utility even if the target state is expected to be visited in the future
limits: Grid-world simulation; exact form for deterministic MDPs. Subfield 04 covers this paper in depth; here only its link to Dyna.
agent_relevance: A concrete ranking rule for which stored subgoals to re-run: expected improvement in the decision times how likely we are to need it. A cheap proxy is recent failures times frequency of use.

source: Karlsson & Frank (2009) Awake replay of remote experiences in the hippocampus. Nat Neurosci 12:913-918
finding: Rat hippocampal place-cell sequences from a previous environment are replayed during pauses in waking behaviour in a different environment, as often as local replay. Remote replay is more likely after recent motion than after long immobility.
numbers: 3 rats. Remote replay in the rest box: 5/22, 149/346, 102/212 events (each above 5% chance, p<.05). Awake 44.1% vs quiescent 35.7% of 1046 candidate events (Z=3.36 p<.001); for immobility over 60 s, 34.2% (106/310), Z=2.88 p<.005. Run sessions in E1: 47%.
limits: Three rats, spatial task. Replay defined by sequence statistics on sharp-wave-ripple events. Shows remote replay exists, not that it updates values.
agent_relevance: Biological precedent for replaying old episodes, not only the latest. Supports replaying old library items.

source: Liu, Dolan, Kurth-Nelson, Behrens (2019) Human replay spontaneously reorganizes experience. Cell 178:640-652
finding: MEG in humans: spontaneous sequential reactivation at rest follows a learned structural rule rather than the experienced order. Structure codes precede object codes. Replay coincides with hippocampal ripple-band power.
numbers: Two studies: n=21 and n=22 analysed. Rule-application quiz accuracy 94.44% (study 1) and 73.1% (study 2), both p<.0001 vs chance 50%. Structure codes lead object codes t(20)=6.47 p<.0001. Decoding betas: sequence code 2.00+-0.12, stimulus code 2.59+-0.1, position code 1.02+-0.09, all p<.0001. Ripple-band power increase at replay onset, permutation p<.05 corrected.
limits: Replay of an arbitrary object ordering task, not a decision task. No test that this replay changes later choices.
agent_relevance: Replay is not a verbatim re-run: it rearranges items by learned structure. Offline simulation in the scaffold should work on abstracted, structure-sorted entries, not raw transcripts.

source: Vikbladh, Meager, King, Blenkinsop, Dolan, Daw, Burgess et al. (2019) Hippocampal contributions to model-based planning and spatial memory. Neuron 102:683-693
finding: Patients with unilateral anterior temporal lobectomy including hippocampal resection were impaired at model-based planning and at place memory. The planning deficit scaled with right hippocampal lesion size, and planning and boundary-driven place memory co-varied in controls but less so in patients.
numbers: 19 patients and 19 healthy controls, no group IQ difference. About 54 to 63% of the hippocampus resected on average. Right-lateralised patients had larger overall lesions than left (t17=-2.61, p=.018).
limits: Patient study; lesions include other anterior temporal tissue. Shows the hippocampus is needed for model-based planning, not that replay is the mechanism.
agent_relevance: Weak support for a link between the memory store and planning. It does not test the Dyna claim itself.

source: Gershman, Markman & Otto (2014) Retrospective revaluation in sequential decision making: a tale of two systems. J Exp Psychol Gen 143:182-194 (as described in Momennejad 2018 and Russek 2017)
finding: Cited by all later papers as the behavioural base: humans can revalue earlier choices after later reward changes, and manipulations affecting rest periods influence their ability to solve integrative decision tasks.
numbers: Not extracted: article text was not opened this session.
limits: Second-hand description only.
agent_relevance: The paradigm (learn, relearn the end, probe the start) is the one to copy when testing a replay step in the scaffold.

source: Foster & Wilson (2006) Reverse replay of behavioural sequences in hippocampal place cells during the awake state. Nature 440:680-683
finding: Cited in this literature as the founding rodent result: reverse-order replay of place-cell sequences at the end of a run on a linear track, in the awake state, right after reward.
numbers: Not extracted: not opened this session.
limits: Second-hand only.
agent_relevance: Reverse-from-the-outcome order is the standard offline order. The schema could replay a failed solution backwards from the failing step.

source: Sutton (1990/1991) Dyna, an integrated architecture for learning, planning, and reacting. SIGART Bulletin 2:160-163
finding: Original Dyna: add a learned model to a model-free learner and update cached values from simulated transitions drawn from the model between real steps. Described in Momennejad (2020) as simulated experience from a model-based learner updating cached value in a model-free learner offline.
numbers: Not extracted: URL returned an error page, original text not read. Maze numbers are in a01.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Core design: one loop for acting and planning; the planner needs only the model and a value cache.

source: Aminmansour, Jafferjee, Imani, Talvitie, Bowling, White (2024) Mitigating value hallucination in Dyna-style planning via multistep predecessor models. JAIR 80:441-473 (arXiv:2006.04363)
finding: Dyna's failure mode with learned models: updating values of REAL states toward values of SIMULATED states can give misleading action values (Hallucinated Value Hypothesis). They define 4 Dyna variants (successor or predecessor model; one-step or multi-step update) and propose a predecessor model with multi-step updates that never updates real states toward simulated-state values.
numbers: Abstract-level claim plus experiments; per-task scores not extracted in this pass.
quote: updating the values of real states towards values of simulated states can result in misleading action values
limits: Models are learned from the agent's own data. Tests are small control tasks.
agent_relevance: Model errors become false memories. In the scaffold, replay must not push a model's invented result into the library as if it were observed; write back only checked outcomes.

source: Holland, Talvitie, Bowling (2018) The effect of planning shape on Dyna-style planning in high-dimensional state spaces (arXiv:1806.01825)
finding: One-step Dyna on Atari (ALE) gave surprisingly little benefit over simply doing more updates on existing real experience, even with a perfect model. Fewer, longer rollouts (different planning shape) help much more, with perfect and learned models. Authors report the first successful use of a learned dynamics model for planning in the ALE.
numbers: Six Atari games in the main test; DQN vs Dyna-DQN with matched total updates. Per-game scores not extracted.
quote: the model must be used to generate unfamiliar experience
limits: Image-based games, DQN learner.
agent_relevance: A near-null result for simple deep Dyna: simulation adds value only when it creates unfamiliar experience. Replaying the same trace again is no better than more training on it.

source: Janner, Fu, Zhang, Levine (2019) When to trust your model: model-based policy optimization (MBPO), arXiv:1906.08253
finding: Short model-generated rollouts branched from real states keep the sample efficiency of model-based methods while matching the asymptotic performance of the best model-free algorithms. Theory: long rollouts compound model error.
numbers: Abstract-level: more sample-efficient than prior model-based methods and matches asymptotic performance of the best model-free algorithms; per-task numbers not extracted.
quote: short model-generated rollouts branched from real data
limits: Continuous control benchmarks, learned ensemble models.
agent_relevance: Short branches from real starting points are safer than long imagined chains. In a scaffold, branch short from a verified state.

source: Schaul, Quan, Antonoglou, Silver (2016) Prioritized experience replay (arXiv:1511.05952)
finding: Replaying transitions with large TD error more often, with importance-sampling correction, improves DQN learning speed over uniform replay.
numbers: Prioritized-replay DQN outperformed uniform-replay DQN on 41 of 49 Atari games.
limits: Atari, DQN. The sampling bias must be corrected.
agent_relevance: The deep-learning version of prioritized sweeping works: sample stored cases by error and correct for the bias this introduces.

source: Yu, Peng, Xu, Galley, Cheng, Nath, Gao, Yu (2025) Dyna-Think: synergizing reasoning, acting and world-model simulation in AI agents (arXiv:2506.00320)
finding: An LLM-agent paper that uses Dyna by name. Dyna-Think Imitation Learning (DIT) distills R1's thinking down to the world-model-simulation parts. Dyna-Think Dyna Training (DDT) trains next-state prediction or critique generation (world model), then the policy. On OSWorld a 32B model reaches best-of-n similar to R1 with 2x fewer tokens.
numbers: OSWorld, 174 tasks (123 in-domain, 51 out), 3 runs, Qwen2.5-32B base. Avg success: GPT-4o 16.5+-2.5; Qwen32B 14.2+-2.2; o3-mini 20.5+-1.4; R1 31.2+-1.4; DIT(R1) 22.6+-1.0; best DDT 26.6+-1.5. Best-of-n all tasks: R1 44.8; DIT 35.6; DDT variants 38.5 to 44.3. WindowsAgentArena avg success: Qwen-32B 23.9+-1.1; R1 26.9+-1.5; DIT 26.9+-1.3; DIT+RFT 28.4+-1.8.
quote: using critique generation for world model training is effective to improving policy performance
limits: Trains weights, which our approach does not. R1 still beats the 32B student on average success (31.2 vs 26.6). The Dyna part is training-time, not offline replay at inference.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue, but it moves the simulation into weights. A scaffold-only agent can borrow the critique-of-predicted-next-state step, not the training.

source: Replay-disruption evidence as summarised in Mattar & Daw 2018 (primary disruption studies not opened)
finding: The theory papers state the causal evidence comes from disruption: blocking replay slows learning without abolishing it. The Mattar & Daw model reproduces this because a model-free agent still learns, only slower.
numbers: No effect sizes reported in these secondary descriptions.
quote: disruption of replay slows down learning without abolishing it completely
limits: Second-hand. The primary rodent ripple-disruption studies were not read this session; flagged as a gap for another angle.
agent_relevance: Replay is an accelerator, not a necessity. Test the scaffold's replay step as an ablation, expecting a speed or budget gain, not a new capability.

source: Sutton & Barto (2018) ch. 8 notes - priority directions and later work
finding: Book notes: prioritized sweeping was developed simultaneously and independently by Moore & Atkeson and Peng & Williams (1993, Queue-Dyna). Later work includes McMahan & Gordon 2005 and van Seijen & Sutton 2013 small backups, which choose the order of single-transition updates to beat prioritized sweeping. The book defines backward focusing (predecessors of changed states) and forward focusing (states reachable from frequently visited ones).
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Bibliographic statements by the textbook authors.
agent_relevance: The two directions of focus map onto two ways to pick library items to re-run: those that feed a changed result, and those likely to be used next.

source: Momennejad (2020) - policy dependence and prioritisation in the review
finding: The review says a human fMRI study found larger unsigned prediction errors were followed by more offline replay, and replay of predecessors of PE-tagged states correlated with later revaluation, more strongly where revaluation was needed. It links SR-Dyna to place-field skew toward goals, because prioritised replay toward goals raises expected visitation there.
numbers: Summarises the eLife 2018 study (n=24; rho=0.54 vs -0.13).
limits: Review-level; the skew explanation is an interpretation.
agent_relevance: Same as a12 and a13.
